newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-SAfrica rate cut seen by Q3, bonds strong.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-SAfrica rate cut seen by Q3, bonds strong.

text.p: South African interest rates are expected to be cut by at least one percentage point by the third quarter of 1997, according to results from Reuters second quarterly poll of economists released on Thursday.

The survey shows that just over half of the economists polled still hold out the hope of a second quarter rate cut, and a large majority are confident prime will be cut from the present level of 20.25 percent by the third quarter.
The median for the second quarter was 19.25 percent and the average 19.72 percent, while the median and average for the third quarter were 19.25 percent and 19.30 percent respectively.
In November, the Reuters poll results also showed a median of 19.25 percent in both the second and third quarters of this year.

Economists say the timing of a cut will be determined by what progress is made in taming inflation, reining in burgeoning money supply and credit growth and what the impact of the latest moves to liberalise exchange controls will be.

"I think (Reserve Bank Governor Chris) Stals is pretty concerned about two things -- inflation and the growth in money supply and bank credit," South African Chamber of Business director of economic policy Ben van Rensburg said.
"Until those show they've taken a turn for the better we won't see a rate cut. My guess is it will not happen until the third quarter."
Inflation is expected to peak at around 10 percent late in the first quarter or early in the second quarter as the final effects of the rand's depreciation come through.

The survey shows inflation is expected to average 9.6 percent in the first quarter, followed by 9.4 percent in the second and 8.8 in the third. For the year as a whole, economists expect inflation to average 8.9 percent.

High money supply and credit extension growth, which rose a preliminary 16.89 percent and 17.07 percent year-on-year respectively in January, were also expected to taper off in the second quarter, economists said.
Rand Merchant Bank Treasury economist Julia Roy said Stals was also likely to wait to see the effects of exchange control easing for individuals on July 1 before cutting rates.
The removal of exchange controls which affect individuals, including increased travel allowances and holding foreign currency accounts, come into effect on July 1.
"Stals will look to see whether there is a flurry around that time. If he cuts rates beforehand he will have used his ammunition," Roy said.
Boland Bank economist Francois Jansen agreed, but said that Stals was likely to be extra cautious and delay a cut until the fourth quarter.
"I think he needs at least two months to get a feel of what the magnitude of the capital flows are, so I would look to the fourth quarter," Jansen said.
Economists said the combined effects of lower inflation, money supply and interest rates would also lead to strong gains on the bond market.
The survey showed the R150 long-bond yield was expected to hit 14.63 percent by the end of the second quarter, followed by 14.23 percent in the third and end the year at 14.15 percent.
In early Thursday trade, R150 was trading at around 15.15 percent.
